title: Cortisol, Perceived Stress, and Schema Modes in Adolescents: A Biopsychosocial Perspective
abstract: ABSTRACT Schema modes represent adaptive or maladaptive responses to life situations, integrating emotional, cognitive, and behavioral dimensions. Adolescence is a critical developmental stage marked by increased stress due to biological, psychological, and social changes. This study aimed to examine whether perceived stress and salivary cortisol are associated with the activation of schema modes in adolescents. A total of 73 participants aged 15–19 were divided into two groups: Group 0 ( n = 37), without symptoms of perceived stress, and Group 1 ( n = 36), with perceived stress symptoms. The findings confirmed that adolescents with higher perceived stress exhibited significantly greater activation of maladaptive schema modes. Additionally, elevated cortisol levels were associated with specific maladaptive modes. In contrast, healthy schema modes, particularly the happy child mode, were linked to lower levels of both perceived stress and cortisol. The perception of stress symptoms emerged as a key predictor for most of the schema modes that showed statistical significance, highlighting the importance of subjective stress appraisal in adolescent psychological functioning. These results underscore the relevance of stress perception in the activation of schema modes and suggest that strengthening healthy modes may be beneficial for promoting mental well‐being in adolescents.
